new_statements.quote: In Pomabamba, just on the other side of the hill, so to speak (a ConQ area), Larsen and Phelps (circa 1975) report that "stress is on the penultimate syllable with few exceptions." [p.195] ... In ConQ, word-level main stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable, secondary stress on the initial syllable, and tertiary stresses on alternating syllables preceding the penult. [p.196] ... Since final long vowels usually attract main stress when following a short penult, the metrical rules accomodate themselves economically to the realities of the language. [p.201] ... Stress always falls on the penultimate syllable in words ending in two heavy syllables [p.203]
new_statements.citation: Stewart, Anne M. 1984. New approaches to coping with stress: A case study in Conchucos Quechua. Work Papers of the Summer Institute of Linguistics, University of North Dakota Session 28: 193-212. DOI 10.31356/silwp.vol28.06.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the penultimate syllable (with a secondary prominence on the word-initial syllable). Weight effects per Stewart: a word-final long vowel (e.g. 1st-person length) following a light penult usually/optionally takes main stress instead, but the penult keeps it when the last two syllables are both heavy; in trisyllabic words a heavy (long or closed) penult is always stressed, otherwise stress is often initial (penult ~ initial variation in all-light trisyllables). For Pomabamba (North Conchucos proper) the reported rule is simply penultimate 'with few exceptions', and Hintz 2000 (whose comparison includes Pomabamba) confines initial stress to Corongo/Huaylas/Huaraz with penult everywhere else in Ancash.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stewart: secondary stress on the word-initial syllable, tertiary stresses alternating right-to-left on syllables preceding the penult; long vowels and diphthongs always attract (at least) secondary stress. Hintz 2000 fn.20 restates this for Huari: main penult, secondary initial.
new_statements.exceptions: Final long vowel after light penult may take main stress (optional 'quantity-sensitivity suppression'); -shkaa '1st person perfect' always main-stressed; some trisyllables lexically initial-stressed (e.g. mallaqay); -kuna 'plural', -kaq 'definitivizer', often -pis 'also' behave as separate words for stress; clitic-like -pita 'ablative', -lla, -lla-raq, -ta 'acc', -na 'now', sometimes -qa 'topic' can be extrametrical, yielding surface antepenultimate stress; stress domain can span two words (Achikay mikukuskinaa). Parker 1976 adds for Ancash generally: interjections stressed on the final syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexical) stress from texts, isolated words and phrases; Stewart notes the phonological word for stress need not equal the syntactic word (two-word domains; level-ordered suffixes outside the domain). No statement about citation-form vs phrase-final differences for Conchucos (Hintz 2000's sentence-final penult shift is stated for Corongo only).
new_statements.identity_note: Stewart 1984 describes 'ConQ' = 'the Quechua of Conchucos, spoken in the eastern portion of the Department of Ancash' (fieldwork 1979-82), i.e. the whole Conchucos dialect chain before the North (qxn, nort2979) / South (qxo, sout2992) split came into use (Diane Hintz 2007:68 fn.14). She explicitly counts Pomabamba (the core of nort2979) as 'a ConQ area', but her own examples carry South-Conchucos suffix shapes (-noo 'simulative', -choo 'locative' = Hintz 2000's Huari forms, versus Pomabamba -naw/-chaw), and Daniel Hintz 2000:116 fn.20 attributes Stewart 1984a to HR = Huari (South Conchucos). So Stewart's first-hand generalization most safely belongs to the chain/South Conchucos; the strictly North-Conchucos (Pomabamba, Piscobamba, N. San Luis, Yanama) evidence is (i) Larsen & Phelps c.1975 quoted by Stewart p.195 (penult, few exceptions), (ii) Hintz 2000 p.58/fn.19, a first-hand comparative statement whose focal varieties include Pomabamba: initial stress only in Corongo/Huaylas/Huaraz, penult elsewhere, (iii) Parker 1976 sec. 2.4 'la mayor parte de Ancash'. All three agree on penultimate. Note also that for South Conchucos Diane Hintz 2006 ranks the two prominences inversely (initial primary, penult secondary), so the primary/secondary labelling in Conchucos is analyst-dependent; Sihuas (sihu1235) and Corongo (coro1247) are separate glottocodes and not covered here.

sources.note: Comparative study whose focal varieties include PB = Pomabamba = North Conchucos (Pomabamba, Mariscal Luzuriaga, N. Fitzcarrald, E. Yungay, Huacrachuco; sources Parker y Chavez 1976, Wroughton 1985, Hintz 1989). p.58: 'El acento en posicion inicial (18c) solo se encuentra en el QCG, HS y HZ en la parte occidental de Ancash'; p.116 fn.19: 'El acento basicamente recae en la penultima silaba en todas las variedades del quechua salvo en el QCG, el HS y el HZ'; fn.20 cites Stewart 1984a:196 as describing HR (Huari = South Conchucos): main stress penult, secondary initial.

sources.citation: Parker, Gary J. 1976. Gramatica quechua: Ancash-Huailas. Lima: Ministerio de Educacion / Instituto de Estudios Peruanos.
sources.note: sec. 2.4 p.57: 'En la mayor parte de Ancash, del mismo modo que en virtualmente todas las variedades del quechua, la intensidad (acento) es mas fuerte en la penultima silaba de cada palabra' (exceptions: interjections with final stress; small class of final-stressed noun roots; word-final long 1st-person vowel may attract stress); the shift toward initial stress is described only for the Callejon de Huaylas. sec. 1.2 pp.28-29 explicitly includes the Conchucos lects in the grammar's scope.
